headline: Opposition walkout as bills on enforced disappearance and NHRC passed
summary: Opposition MPs protested with black cloths over their mouths, alleging the laws are 'weakened' and provide unequal rules for rights violations.
details: Parliament passed three major bills on Sunday, including the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, 2026, and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Bill, 2026, amid strong opposition dissent.
Opposition MPs, including those from Jamaat, walked out of the House before the passage of the rights bills, with some wearing black cloths over their mouths to signal their protest.

The Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill assigns the responsibility for investigating such cases to the police, with designated officers usually of sub-inspector rank leading the probes.
The NHRC Bill contains measures to strengthen the commission but limits its power to directly investigate allegations of human rights violations committed by disciplined forces.
A third piece of legislation, the Transfer of Property (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was also passed, allowing donors to retain lifetime usage rights when gifting property to family members.
The opposition had previously boycotted discussions on these bills in parliamentary standing committees, claiming the legislation was too weak to effectively protect human rights.
The bills were passed by voice vote after the opposition leader, Shafiqur Rahman, announced the walkout and the Speaker refused to grant him further floor time during the property bill vote.
caption:
Opposition MPs walked out of Parliament with black cloths over their mouths to protest 'weakened' human rights bills.

Parliament passed three major bills on Sunday, including the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, 2026, and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Bill, 2026, amid strong opposition dissent.

The Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill assigns the responsibility for investigating such cases to the police, with designated officers usually of sub-inspector rank leading the probes.

The NHRC Bill contains measures to strengthen the commission but limits its power to directly investigate allegations of human rights violations committed by disciplined forces.

A third piece of legislation, the Transfer of Property (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was also passed, allowing donors to retain lifetime usage rights when gifting property to family members.

The opposition had previously boycotted discussions on these bills in parliamentary standing committees, claiming the legislation was too weak to effectively protect human rights.

The bills were passed by voice vote after the opposition leader, Shafiqur Rahman, announced the walkout and the Speaker refused to grant him further floor time during the property bill vote.

headline_marked: TIB warns [[new SRB force could become another Rab]], citing lack of reform
headline: TIB warns new SRB force could become another Rab, citing lack of reform
summary: Transparency International Bangladesh says changing the name of the force alone won't bring institutional reform and warns of potential human rights violations.
details: Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has expressed concern that the proposed Special Response Battalion (SRB) Bill, 2026 could create a force similar to the Rapid Action Battalion (Rab) under a new name.
TIB warns that the draft law contains provisions giving the force broad and unclear powers, including the ability to conduct searches and arrests without warrants based on suspicion.

Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman stated that while abolishing Rab was a long-awaited step, simply changing the name will not bring institutional reform without changes to structure, personnel, and accountability.
The organization called for the removal of provisions allowing armed forces members to join the SRB on deputation to prevent the use of military tactics in internal policing.
TIB criticized the plan to transfer Rab personnel to the SRB without a vetting process, insisting that those accused of extrajudicial killings, torture, or enforced disappearances must be excluded.
Concerns were raised over vague terms like 'maintaining internal security,' which TIB says could be misused to suppress dissent or provide legal cover for human rights violations.

TIB also questioned the proposed complaints mechanism, arguing that allegations against force members should be investigated by an independent civilian oversight authority rather than their own colleagues.
The organization urged the government to consult experts and stakeholders to establish a genuinely reformed law-enforcement institution.
